source.title: Interpreting Adversarial Examples by Activation Promotion and Suppression
source.authors: Kaidi Xu; Si-Jia Liu; Gaoyuan Zhang; Meng-Shu Sun; Pu Zhao; Quan-Fu Fan; Chuang Gan; X. Lin

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how hidden-unit semantic interpretability relates to sensitivity to adversarial attacks, but it does not measure whether individual units respond to several unrelated inputs or test the claim versions about polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The network-dissection results concern unit interpretability and changes under adversarial perturbations, not whether a unit has multiple unrelated meanings. The neuron-masking robustness results do not test the claim. No result cited from other work is recorded as a study result.
record.test_reason: The study analyses adversarial perturbations at pixel, image and unit level and links unit sensitivity to network-dissection interpretability. It never measures whether units respond to several unrelated inputs, how common that is, or what causes it. Its only nod is a remark that one unit might detect multiple concepts, used to average IoU over concepts. It neither tests nor uses polysemanticity; 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses', since polysemanticity is barely mentioned.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that adversarial perturbations show a promotion-suppression effect tied to CAM discriminative regions. They also report that masking sensitive interpretable units improves adversarial robustness at slight clean-accuracy cost. They draw no conclusion about polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses network dissection to analyze semantic interpretability and adversarial sensitivity; it does not apply the original polysemanticity methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sensitivity–interpretability relationship varies with layer depth and the number N of top-ranked sensitive units.

fits_no_version.finding: In Resnet 152, the top-N adversarially sensitive units have higher mean network-dissection IoU than random units (p<0.05 in most cases), more so in deeper layers and at larger N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Units most sensitive to adversarial perturbations tend to be semantically interpretable concept detectors.

fits_no_version.finding: Among the 100 most sensitive units, low-level color/texture detectors dominate shallow layers and object/part detectors dominate deep layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept categories of adversarially sensitive units shift from low- to high-level with depth.

record.problems: The study does not measure whether units respond to multiple unrelated inputs. The detector counts in Figure 9(b) are not stated numerically in the text; the reported p-value result is described only as holding in most cases.
record.rows_left_out: The neuron-masking results in Appendix 4, Table A2 concern adversarial robustness and clean accuracy, not polysemanticity. Pixel- and image-level adversarial-attack analyses likewise do not measure the claim's neuron-level behavior.

untested.parts: Whether image-classifier units respond to several unrelated inputs; detectors are labelled only by their top concept.
No analysis of initialization, regularization or noise.
No architecture or activation-function comparison of polysemanticity.
Uses a fixed top-5% activation threshold and IoU>0.04; no test of how the polysemantic label depends on these choices.

record.verdict_notes: Changed relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The only polysemanticity-adjacent text is the remark that a unit might detect multiple concepts, used as a definitional step, not measured. Neither original source is used.

versions.untested_parts: Whether image-classifier neurons respond strongly to several unrelated inputs.
Language-model MLP neurons and the prevalence of responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Whether architecture, activation function, or regularization changes polysemanticity, and whether it can be reduced without large performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related offshoots rather than unrelated features.
Whether polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: Resnet 152
rows.operation_detail: Compared semantic interpretability of top-ranked adversarially sensitive units with the background distribution of randomly selected units.
rows.measure: p-value for the interpretability (IoU) of the top N units ranked by adversarial sensitivity
rows.baseline: IoU distribution of randomly selected units
rows.note: The text says the connection becomes more significant as N increases and is stronger in deeper layers. This measures sensitivity versus concept interpretability, not multiple unrelated meanings per unit.
rows.check: Measures significance of the sensitivity-interpretability association, not polysemanticity. The value 'p < 0.05 in most cases' is from the figure description and is not read per layer or N. State should stay cannot_determine.

rows.subject: Resnet 152
rows.operation_detail: Counted concept detectors among the 100 most adversarially sensitive units in each layer.

conditions.value: color, texture, material, part, object, scene

rows.measure: Number of concept detectors by concept category
rows.note: The text describes low-level concepts as more prevalent in lower layers and high-level concepts, including object and part, as more prevalent in deeper layers. It does not report how many unrelated concepts any one unit detects.
rows.check: State 'partial' is unjustified. It counts concept detectors by top-ranked concept category among sensitive units; no version's effect is measured, and the values are figure-only.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
